title: Playing mostly for White dancers
summary: Most Southwestern dances were White, and the White crowds only wanted St. Louis Blues; Smith describes Little Rock and Ritz Ballroom jobs.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: When you were working in the Texas area, say, or Oklahoma, and you'd do one-nighters, and you'd go to some little town and
there'd be a ballroom where you'd be booked...
Would you have White people and Black people there?
No. There would only be Black or either White. Most of the dances were White -- White places. You had big ballrooms.
For instance, in big ballrooms where there'd be White people dancing, could you play the blues and that sort of stuff for them?

No. "The St. Louis Blues" was the only blues they cared anything about. It's still that today. That's all they like. "The St. Louis Blues." They recognize it. But any other blues, they didn't appreciate it. Just a few of these youngsters now... Nowadays, you can play a little blues for them.
I'm curious about this, because there's obviously something I don't understand. I was imagining that when you were working the South, you were mainly playing for Black people.

No. No! Most of them...90 percent of them were White. And we played a lot of... We used to go to Little Rock, worked about two or three years out there at a place kind of like a carnival. They'd run it all the summer. And we worked there every night, except we was off on Sunday night. Then we'd leave there and go back to Oklahoma City and played another place there called the Ritz Ballroom. All of that was White. We worked
there all winter. Then we had five days off to get back to Little Rock. That's really it.
